utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And General Talic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you in a language that I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, assisted by Susan Grogan, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Tanja Radosavljevic, and I'd like to introduce to Your Honours Milan Trbojevic, who's in the process of becoming new co-counsel for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Good morning to you. Appearance for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. I'm Michel Pitron representing General Talic, assisted by Natasha Fauveau -- with Natasha Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good morning to you. Any preliminaries before we bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's a question of timetabling really that I want to raise. I notice that at the moment we're not supposed to be sitting again this Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's not our fault.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I know that, yes. Your Honour, I was wondering -- I don't know whether it is court maintenance or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was wondering whether there was the slightest remotest possibility that that could be put off until the next time because we were unable to stop the next witness coming when we tried -- when it was realised that cross-examination was going to take longer than was anticipated. So he's here. If we're only going to sit three days this week, I gather from what -- I've spoken to Defence counsel, it may well be that Judge Draganovic is going to take the rest -- until Thursday. Now, it is very expensive to fly these witnesses here and to keep them. And if there was the remotest possibility that we could at least start him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, that obviously, Ms. Korner -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You know, I'm raising it so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends very little on us, because it's not my style or the wish of my colleagues to interfere much in either the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination, provided relevant questions are being asked. Therefore, it's not our intention to cut short --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's number one. And secondly, court maintenance is, I think, something that is organisational that we cannot touch. Like, we couldn't touch last Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that. There was something different. But it seems to me that court maintenance, A, doesn't take very long, as far as I'm aware. And to shut down a whole session for that does seem to me, given the competing interests, one of which is the expense, that perhaps an exception could be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. We will check.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the break. But I'm not exactly that hopeful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Well, I'm not either. But if you don't try, you won't succeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, perhaps it might be worth thinking about sending this witness back, because it's -- and bringing him back again towards the end of the week. A briefing would have taken place in any case, so he would only need to be here the day before starting evidence. That would save you having to keep him here between now and, say, Saturday. You know, I mean -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They -- as I understand it, people who come from Bosnia have to be flown here on Friday. They can't be flown here on the weekend. And he came in on Friday. Don't ask me why, Your Honour. But as far as I understand the VWS -- I think it's maybe the cost of staffing, keeping them working over the weekend. So that would mean that if he goes back, say, tomorrow, he'd have to come back again on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But that would save you -- I don't know whether it's worth its while.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know either, Your Honour. All I'm saying is -- and I appreciate Your Honours have limited control over things like court maintenance -- is that it does seem to me that if the -- it can be arranged, then it would cost less in terms of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will check and I will try. In the meantime perhaps one of my staff -- Inneke, please, you could start checking on it and by the time we have the break, maybe we'll have an idea of where we are, because I don't even know exactly who to approach on such a matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour. I'm just raising it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the obvious proper choice based upon my conversations with Ms. Fauveau this morning and my own preparation over the last several days is to send this witness home. There's -- I don't think there's any chance we're going to reach him this week. We could have an hour maybe on Thursday if we're lucky. And it's hardly worth keeping him here a week to do that. The other thing -- one makes plans based upon what understand the schedule of our sittings to be. And last minute changes cause chaos. So I'm not very enthusiastic about Ms. Korner's suggestion that we work out a way to sit on Friday? Because it would cause me to have to change some things that I had planned, and I'd just as soon not do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Draganovic -- or Judge Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. While things are being set up, could I just ask that if reference is going to be made to things said on previous days the transcript reference could be given, the page number. I'd be very grateful. It's helpful if one can see the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Good morning, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed with the solemn declaration that you are familiar with, please. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Please, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Ms. Fauveau-Ivanovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of the hearing of the 16th of May, we were speaking about the debris left over from a bomb that you found at the site of the crime. And on the 24th of April -- and it's page 4888 of the French transcript. You said that in almost all cases these bombs came from the JNA arsenals. On the 16th of May -- it's page 68 of the LiveNote -- you said that some of this debris was of military origin. Among the debris that you found, was there any debris that was not of military origin?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to say that I didn't mention all the cases of explosions, although that -- although in most cases I went to carry out on-site investigations as an investigative judge. I said that these were bombs of military origin from the JNA arsenal, and I stand by this claim now. If you want to know how I determined this, I'll tell you. But if not, I won't say anything. But I can claim this because I wasn't the only person to carry out this on-site investigation. A police team accompanied me. It was a criminalistics team. They were people who knew about these explosives. And on the basis of what -- what was determined, I came to these conclusions. These were criminal inspectors of Serbian nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 24th of April -- it's page 4888 -- you said that this debris came from a factory of military materiel which is located in Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were various types of explosive devices. I said that there were hand grenades too. They were called Kasikara. General Talic understands this term very well. These bombs were produced in the military factory in Bugojno before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that this factory that produced military material was like all the other factories at the time, a socially owned factory?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were military factories which produced these special-purpose products and they were state-owned. I know that no one else was able to obtain explosive devices other than the JNA or that is to say, the army and the police. I don't know how the police managed to do this. I think that it was in a position to do this. It was carried out in accordance with the laws that were in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that this factory also provided weapons to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence, I assume it had its own weapons. But this was all under the control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the weapons from these -- from this factory could be in the army and the police and in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 24th of April, on the hearing on that date -- and we're still referring to page 4888 -- you said that there were no prosecutions against the perpetrators of these explosions. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that. So after the on-site investigations, the public security station had the task -- or the police had the task of finding out who the perpetrators were, as far as I can remember -- not a single case was detected at that time. So that means right up to the time of my arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you spoken to the prosecutor about these explosions?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After each case of that kind, I and the prosecutor would usually go to carry out the on-site investigation together. Or in any event, we would speak about the case, and I would not only speak to the prosecutor about it but also to the chief of the public security station and the chief of the criminal -- the crime department. On several occasions, Majkic Dragan, who was the chief of the police of the public security station, I spoke to him and complained about this to him and also to the chief of the crime department. And this was something I also did at meetings in the municipality, which were attended by the person who was then the president of the municipality, Nedeljko Rasula. I pointed out that this was a problem, and I requested that more active means be undertaken to discover the perpetrators of these excesses. I also pointed out that -- I also expressed my opinion that this was not a problem, that it wasn't a problem to discover who the perpetrators were, because this was taking place very often. In April and in May there were explosions which occurred almost every evening. And this was -- this would take place in Bosniak flats, cars, et cetera. There was one excess, one incident, two shells were fired at a mosque in Donji Komengrad. This caused problems and fear among the local population. One shell hit a well, and I think it damaged it. I don't know what the caliber of these shells was. The second shell did not explode. But we found it in a nearby field. It was planted in the ground. And that also came from the JNA arsenal. And we know where these shells were fired from. They were fired from a position -- well in a village above --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question was quite simple. I simply asked you whether you had spoken to the prosecutor about these explosions.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me who was the Prosecutor in Sanski Most at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think that's the question that's been translated to the witness. I think the question was what the name --

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. Mrs. Faveau asked what the name of the prosecutor was and the translation was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the advantage of not having --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was listening to the question. But Your Honour, if we're not -- I think it is important to remind the interpreters that we had this problem before when Madam Fauveau checked the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be much asking you, Madam Fauveau, if it's not of an inconvenience to you -- I know that you understand the witness's language. If you could perhaps put on the earphones as well so that -- I don't know. I mean, if it's an inconvenience, don't do it. But perhaps you will be the one in the best position to know if your -- the interpretation is the correct one or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But that means that I would be listening to another language from the one that I am speaking. I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, actually, I'm not concentrating on your French. I'm concentrating on the English translation, that interpretation they I get. So I wouldn't know if there is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm doing this deliberately because I don't want there to be a repetition of what happened last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact I appreciate that very much, Ms. Korner. Thanks. So the question was not as was translated in English at the time. But it seems that Madam Fauveau would like to know who the prosecutor was, his name, in other words, in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The prosecutor's name was Mr. Slobodan Milasinovic. And his assistant was Enver Ceric, his deputy. Milasinovic was of Serbian nationality, and Enver Ceric, who was unfortunately killed, was a Bosniak. And I was very much in contact with them, every day, and we would speak about these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the prosecutor make a request for the investigations to be completed? And I'm talking about investigative proceedings.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you think that this request was put to the Court, no. It was not. But I assume that he did ask the police in writing to work on discovering the perpetrators of such actions. As I've already said, this was a period -- this was actually the period between April and May. It's a very brief period. So I don't think there were any court investigations. Actually, I seem to be remembering right now. At that time Mr. Milasinovic term of office was expiring or had just expired. So that was a problem too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but about an incident in Milin Birt, in which a young Muslim was seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at the site when this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not on the site when the incident occurred. However, I did carry out the subsequent on-site investigation. That is to say, when I was informed about the incident, in the morning hours of the following day, that is. I carried out the on-site investigation, and I was in this unit. I talked to the officers of that unit and to the soldiers who were there at that particular point. These were members of the 6th Krajina Brigade [As interpreted]. I can't remember now. It was a battalion, actually. But I have it written down, so probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who informed you about the fact that this incident took place?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to remember now who informed me, but I imagined that it was the duty service of the public security station that informed me. That is what they do by way of procedure after such incidents. So I assume that they informed me that this incident had occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the headquarters of the command of this brigade, in what capacity did you go there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appear there as the judge on duty, as the investigative judge, who came out to carry out the on-site investigation, according to the Law on Criminal Procedure, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was an investigation opened?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no official investigation was opened then, until I was arrested, that is. Now, whether the military prosecutor's office started any kind of investigation, that I don't know. But these were military persons, so they were under the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 24th of April, you said -- and I'm quoting you. It's page 88 -- "I am asking not only for investigations to be initiated but also for there to be prosecutions." Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. I insisted upon that because I really saw for myself on the actual scene that these soldiers who were at the point had committed a crime. That is to say that a citizen who is from there, his house is nearby, and he stopped, and he had to show his ID. And when he already started driving towards his house -- this was after he was checked -- he was shot at, fired at, his vehicle was, from the back, to put it that way. And then it was uncertain as to whether he would be alive or not. He was in a very serious situation. He was hit in the spine, and the vehicle was bullet riddled because it had been shot at from an automatic weapon. I had called for an investigation and for proceedings to be initiated. That's why I went to the command of that unit and that's why I talked to the officers and that's why I insisted that proceedings be initiated against these soldiers. Now, whether such proceedings were indeed instituted, that is something I really do not know. However, there is one thing I do know: This man is alive until the present day. He is seriously disabled. He lives in Sanski Most, and he comes to the courthouse and to the police station until the present day and he seeks criminal proceedings to be instituted. His last name is hue Huzeirovic. I can't remember his first name now. He lives at Milin Birt, which is to say about 50 metres away from the checkpoint. The house is on the left-hand side, if you are looking in the direction of Prijedor. He can even testify to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, under which rule of the proceedings of the criminal court can a judge order that there be -- that proceedings be initiated?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I am a professional judge, but I am here as a witness. It is not necessary for me to answer that question, because you are a lawyer, you are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in April 1992 the Law on Criminal Procedure of Yugoslavia, was still in force?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was still in force. I think there had been some amendments to it, but yes, it was still in force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in accordance with this code a judge can't ask for investigations or proceedings to be instituted? This is a matter for the competence of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had made proposals to that effect, for proceedings to be initiated. It's not that I did it in writing. I did this orally. I had suggested that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Requesting such proceedings, hadn't you abandoned your neutrality as a judge and exceeded your competence?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are really putting a funny question to me. I do not wish to answer such a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, I think without letting this become a storm in a teacup, may I suggest to you to proceed to another question. Judge, please may I -- may I remind you that here in this Tribunal I am the one who decides. And if I will ask you to answer a question, whether you like it or not you will need -- you will be required to answer it. And please avoid going into a direct confrontation with the witness, who's got every right -- with counsel, who's got every right to cross-examine you and put all those questions that are allowed by this Trial Chamber. Thank you. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 24th of April, you spoke about a meeting which took place at the police station in Sanski Most on the 17th of April, 1992. Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that same hearing -- it's page 4925 -- you said -- you quoted what Rasula had said at this meeting. How did you know what Rasula had said if you didn't attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out from people out there, policemen, policemen who were sent out that day, and I found out about that on that very same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following day after this meeting you went to the building of the municipality where Croatian and Muslim policemen had taken shelter. Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there to seek information, to see what had happened, because I was still working as a judge, as the president of the court, and I wanted to get information about that situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that Croatian and Muslim policemen were there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't hard to find out, you see. Everything that happened was heard about and seen immediately, because the courthouse is in the immediate vicinity of the police station, or rather, the public security station and of the municipality building. As a matter of fact, I think I had been informed by telephone about what happened at the public security station. I can't remember now though who informed me about that. But during the course of that day, or rather, that afternoon, I knew that people -- that the policemen who were thrown out of the police station, the public security station, went to the municipality building, to the municipal assembly building, rather. Before that, there was a meeting, but I did not attend it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you enter the building of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was easy for me to enter. It was easy. I came from home that morning in my own car, and I parked in front of the building, in front of the municipal assembly building, and I entered the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslim and Croat police who were in the municipality building, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes. I think so, yes. At the entrance by the door in the hallway I did see these policemen. They were probably guarding the entrance to the building. I think they were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also spoke about a meeting that took place on the 20th of April, 1992. It was a meeting at which General Talic was present. Did you personally attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the hearing on the 15th of May -- it's page 25 of the LiveNote -- you said that this visit by General Talic had not seriously affected the situation in Sanski Most. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember saying that. That was my observation, and I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor show the witness his written statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which one? All of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, preferably. But at the moment, I need the statement from October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry. I handed to him I think the one wrong. I gave him the October 2000. It's October 1999 you want, is it? It says "1992" on the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's October 1999. [Microphone not activated] That's what I heard as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could have it back, then. It's easier if we find it for the witness than the usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at page 10 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You mean in Serbo-Croat. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 10 in the -- in both the English and the Serbo-Croat version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the middle of the page, there's a paragraph which starts with the words "this meeting had no results." If you have a look -- if you go on, you said: [In English] "It was only held to calm down the situation." Have you found this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have. The meeting did not yield any results. The meeting was held only to calm down the situation. Yes. Yes, that's quite clear. You can talk in Bosnian too. I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you wanted to say that the meeting had been convened in order to calm the situation but that it didn't succeed in doing this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Actually, I'll explain this in a single sentence if you want me to. The objective was to have the army, the 6th Krajina Brigade withdraw from town, from the streets, and for it to be disarmed simply. That was the objective of the meeting. However, what happened? Nothing. Actually what happened happened. They occupied the entire town, every street, every crossroads, every neighbourhood. As for their weapons arsenal, they moved them into the hills above town from where they were shelling. That's what I meant when I gave this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness P616.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a report from the command of the 6th Corps of the 20th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, the one I have as Exhibit P616 says 5th, not 6th. I don't know what you said, because again, I'm not following the French.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Fauveau did mention the 5th Corps, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, that would go as 5th and not 6th. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a report from the 5th Corps of the 20th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way it's put here, this is a regular combat report of the command of the 5th Corps of the JNA. And at that time its commander was General Talic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look -- in Serbo-Croat it's page 1, and in the English version it's page 2 -- could you have a look at paragraph 2. It says: [In English] "A team from Corps Commander -- has assessed the situation in the Prijedor region, focussing on Sanski Most and measures are being taken to improve the situation." [Interpretation] Have you found this passage? It's at the bottom of the first page in the Serbo-Croat version.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the hearing on the 15th of May -- it's page 13 of the LiveNote, you said that you weren't aware of the presence of a team from the corps command at Sanski Most. Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't quite understand what you were saying. Could you please repeat it once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, you said that you weren't aware of the presence of a team from the corps command at Sanski Most. Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now I can't remember whether that's the way I had put it. But the 5th Corps -- the 5th Corps, I know that that was the Banja Luka Corps of the JNA. Later on it grew into the 1st Corps of the Serb army. But whether there were some people from the command in Banja Luka, that I don't know. I know for sure though that the representatives -- or rather, the high officers, like the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade, the commander of the staff, they fell under that particular corps. And now how the reporting went, that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you knew that General Talic on the 20th of April -- you knew that he was in Sanski Most on that date.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that, found out about that, knew that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So General Talic was the commander of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew that there was someone from the command of the 5th Corps in Sanski Most on the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Commander Talic was there, and it was -- was he a major? Major Zeljaja from Prijedor. And there was another one, another officer, another officer or two. I don't know. And Commander Basara was there, the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade. That is as far as the military structures are concerned of that corps, that is. Because they are all linked up. They were all linked up within the 5th Corps, the Prijedor Brigade and the Sanska Brigade, and these people were there then. I know they were there. I heard about that. I was informed about that. I mean, I could have been present at the meeting too, but I did not wish to be present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that later you found the diary that belonged to Rasula. Could you tell us where you found this diary.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. I found the diary, whichever word you want to use for it -- Nedeljko Rasula's diary, the then-president of the municipality of Sanski Most and the president of the Crisis Staff or rather the War Staff of the Serb municipality of Sanski Most. I found it in the neighbourhood of Caplje. Do you want me to tell you the exact location more precise than that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Thank you. When did you find this diary?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That diary -- well, I found it during those days. I came to Sanski Most in 1995, and I can't tell you the exact day, but I think -- was it the beginning of November or the end of October? I can't remember the exact day. But it was round there. End of October, beginning of November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness document P759.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that Rasula's diary? Have you found Rasula's diary?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Rasula's diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that this is Rasula's diary?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew Nedeljko Rasula very well. I knew his handwriting. I knew where his house was in Caplje. And that's precisely where I found it. And also, by the contents of the diary, it was easy for me to establish that it was Rasula's diary. There are many entries in the diary that corroborate that. As for his handwriting, I am very familiar with it, since he was a teacher. And I know that he was a rare person among the Serbs in Sanski Most who used the Cyrillic alphabet when he wrote. And he had very nice handwriting. So it was very simple for me to establish that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you found this diary, was someone able to add a few words or a few sentences to this diary which belonged to Rasula, someone other than Rasula obviously.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Because everything I saw written in there was written in his handwriting and according to a certain chronology, except that at the very end there are a few pages that were torn out. Now, when they were torn out, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you find the note which refers to the meeting of the 20th of April, 1992. Before analysing this note, could you confirm that this diary was written in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A minute ago you said that Rasula always wrote in the Cyrillic script; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he wrote in the Cyrillic script most of the time. I do not remember him having written in the Latin script, and I had known him for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the note which refers to the meeting of the 20th of April and which concerns the activities of the JNA. And the words that General Talic allegedly said, "don't ask anyone to come to your help, otherwise you will see that Kupres, Bosanski Brod, and Vukovar." It's at the bottom of the page, of the page which has the date the 5th of November printed in the Serbo-Croat version. Have you found this passage?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found what it says here, "the JNA will guarantee peace and security to the citizens." That's what General Talic said. That is on this page number 5, dated the 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the hearing on the 24th of April, 2002, page 4944, you read that General Talic allegedly said what is said in the diary, "Don't call anyone to your help. Otherwise you will see that Kupres, Bosanski Brod, and Vukovar." Do you still stand by this statement?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I can't read now what I said. I can't read the transcript. But it says here everything that General Talic -- is written here. And he can confirm that or he can deny that. This is Rasula's notes. These are the notes that Rasula took. And I abide by what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have a look at this -- very well -- at this passage, this paragraph. In the middle of what's written in Cyrillic script, there are three words -- at least three words which have been written in the Latin script. "Otherwise" -- the word for that is "inace" in Serbo-Croat. And "you will," which in Serbo-Croat is "vic ete", those are two words, and there is perhaps a third word which I can't read. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see what you've just been saying to me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it written in the Latin script?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "inace," "otherwise," is written in the Latin script. And also down here where it says "vic ete," "you shall."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us why Rasula, who almost always wrote in the Cyrillic script and whose entire diary was written in the Cyrillic script, could you explain to us why he wrote these three words in the Latin script?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you allow for the possibility that someone other than Rasula added these words?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another subject. At the hearing of the 24th of April, 2002, you spoke about isolated snipers -- individual snipers. And you said they were people from the 6th Brigade. It's on page 4939. Did you see these snipers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, did you say 6th Brigade or 5th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: 6th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 6th. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the 6th Krajina Brigade, Your Honour, and the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was watching, and I also knew that at the Hotel Sanus, in the rooms there, there were snipers. They were dressed as soldiers. All the windows were open for the most part across the terraces. So they were there for a longer period of time. In front of the Hotel Sanus or in front of the municipality building, there was -- there was a barricade-type thing, so access was not allowed to the hotel or to the municipality building. And there was a military guard. Should I put it that way? Or rather, soldiers who were there by that barricade. Also, the sniper nest could be seen on the building itself by the post office. That's where the members of the SOS were, up on the building that is next to the post office building. That is both an apartment building and a business building. So they were up on the roof. And sandbags could be seen around, so this place where the sniper nest was, was protected that way. And some people who lived in that building, Bosniaks, informed me about that, that I should be careful when I walk across the square in that area. They also told me the name of the person who was most often at the sniper nest, the person from the SOS. So I knew that for sure, and I saw it too. From the hotel, the snipers controlled the bridge and the centre of town across the bridge on the left bank. That's where a doctor was killed. That's where a doctor was killed, a Bosniak, Mehmed Alagic, on the 27th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the identity of the snipers who belonged to the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 24th of April -- it's page 4980 -- you spoke about the weapons of the Territorial Defence and you said that they had been taken in a violent manner and that that took place from 1991. When you say "in a violent manner," did you mean that members of the Territorial Defence had opposed this action?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I meant. Nobody opposed that action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that when these arms were taken, this was in fact legal action, since you yourself said that a law in the federal assembly had been voted to this effect?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Federal Assembly of Yugoslavia, as far as I can remember, adopted a law according to a shorter procedure -- rather, the law on armed forces was amended. I can't even remember now any more. But this law subordinated the Territorial Defence to the JNA. After that, what happened happened. That is to say, that they took all the weapons of the Territorial Defence. I already said this last time. Trucks came, military trucks of the JNA. I saw these trucks. There were five or six trucks -- I don't know -- at least. All of them military vehicles, the same. The street was blocked. While they were loading the weapons and the equipment on that day. I saw them from the courthouse as they were leaving, this column of vehicles. What I learned, heard, felt was that these weapons were handed over to the 6th Krajina Brigade -- or rather, this is how the Serb people were armed in the area of the municipality of Sanski Most, because first the weapons ended up in Lusci Palanka. This is the information that I could get at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say when this action took place?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I can't remember the exact date, or rather, the time. I think it could have been perhaps even in 1992, but I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness document P19.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read the first paragraph. Sir, it's the very first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me have a look at the document itself. Please allow me to do that. This document is not signed and it has no seal on the last page, number 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In socialist Yugoslavia, up until 1992 did you see many official documents without a signature and without a -- and without a stamp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In socialist Yugoslavia, I think that documents for the most part had a signature and a stamp, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless I would like to ask you to read the first paragraph of this document.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the basis of the order of the head --" I think it says of the Main Staff -- "OS SFRY strictly confidential. 19-1. Dated the 14th of May, 1990, carried out in the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Action of taking over and securing weapons and munition of entities ONO and DSZ, that is total national defence and social self protection in the facilities of the Yugoslav People's Army." I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this document refer to the action of taking arms from the Territorial Defence, the weapons which were taken by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what happened in Sanski Most, that the JNA took the weapons and the equipment of the Territorial Defence of Sanski Most. I think that that was sometime round the beginning of 1992, if I'm not mistaken. And what it says here, I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this document is from the 13th of September, 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a document because it says "Commander -- Lieutenant Colonel General Milos Bajcetic," some general from Belgrade. But there is no signature, no stamp. For me this is not a document. I don't know anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's say that this document has the date the 13th of September, 1990.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to this document -- if we have a look at paragraph 2, the weapons of the Territorial Defence in the Banja Luka region were allegedly taken on the 13th of June, 1990 and in a period before this date; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the JNA took over documents from the TO from a legal point of view, but I am talking about the actual state of affairs, what happened in fact, what I saw with my very own eyes and what I know. And now whether those weapons and equipment were kept in Sanski Most as a JNA arsenal, that I don't know. But I did know that this was for the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, would it be convenient to make a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if Madam Fauveau is leaving that document and the suggestion is meant to be that the document shows that TO weapons were collected by order of the Bosnian government in September 1990, then I would invite her to deal with the witness with the fourth paragraph in translation on page 1, because I think the way it's been left could create a misleading impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, you will take that up after the break, or if you prefer to take it up now, perhaps you could do it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll have a look at that in a minute, if -- immediately if Ms. Korner could tell me where this paragraph is in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first page of the translation which starts: "The action applied to the armaments and ammunition of the Territorial Defence and to other actors only if so desired and explicitly requested."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the order is from 1990 and belongs to the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the only point I'm making is if it's to be left that way with a suggestion that all arms collected were in 1990 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the point has been made. The witness has already answered the question, saying that the only thing that he can testify to is what actually he said given a particular point in time, and I think you have made a point by pointing to paragraph 4 and I think we could leave it a that. And there's no need -- I see no further need for any further question, because it's not going to change the situation in any case. I mean, the witness has already stated that he can only testify as to what happened in 1992 and not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, all I'm concerned about is because of the number of documents in this case, that if it's to be left and potentially it's misleading -- it can just get lost. That's why I'm dealing with it stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. No. I'm thankful for having brought it up, because it's obviously important but once it's been brought up, I don't see any reason for any further questions. So we'll break now for half an hour, resuming at just before 11.00, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 23rd of April, 2002 -- it's page 4873 -- you mentioned a certain Nedeljko Anicic, and you said that this person was the number one in the Main Staff of the 6th Brigade. Do you remember speaking about this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the hearing of the 15th of May, you said that Colonel Anicic led a military team. That is page 14 of the LiveNote of the 15th of May. Could you explain to us what in your opinion is meant by a military team.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly not the way I put it. It was no team. It was an organisation, a military organisation. Nedeljko Anicic was commander of the staff, I think, of the Territorial Defence -- of the Serb Territorial Defence in Sanski Most. He was also on the Crisis Staff -- or rather, the War Staff. He was a retired colonel or lieutenant colonel. I can't remember. I think it was a colonel -- of the JNA. So in 1992 he was there in the command -- in the defence command. In my opinion, in my assessment, he was the man in charge. He was the military officer in charge at the command of the Serb army in Sanski Most, of the Serb defence, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness document P638.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have a look at the first page of this document, can you confirm that this document has a stamp from -- a stamp of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a stamp of the staff of the Territorial Defence of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document also bears the signature of Nedeljko Anicic. And this is on the first page, again.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the brigades of the Territorial Defence -- do you know that they weren't under the command of the 1st Corps until July 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please put that question to me once again, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you confirm that the document that you have in front of you is a document from the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the staff of the Serb Territorial Defence of Sanski Most. Nedeljko Anicic was its commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. We agree. Now my question is: Do you know that the Territorial Defence, the Serbian Territorial Defence, was not under the command until July 1992 -- was not under the command of the 1st Corps until 1 July 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness document DT9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While that's being done, Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman, Madam Fauveau -- because I forgot to tell you straight away upon resuming the sitting -- there's no way we can make use of Friday in this courtroom or any other courtroom, because that's the problem, because it's the maintenance is done on a pretty, seems to me, regularised basis and there won't be any other courtroom available to us, in any case. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should note for the LiveNote that when Madam Fauveau asked the question, she didn't just say July, she said the 1st of July. I thought she had but then I wasn't sure. And all it's come out is until July 1992. It may not make a difference, but in fact she did use the word "the 1st of July."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Madam Fauveau? [Microphone not activated] Does it make a difference to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It was the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We can leave it at that, because the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. We can leave it at that, in any case, because the witness already answered -- told us -- telling us that he did -- he's not in a position to answer that question. Thank you. Please proceed with the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document that you have in front of you, it's an order from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have a look at paragraph 4. This paragraph refers to the Light Brigade of Sanski Most, the Sanski Most Light Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context, Sanski Most is being mentioned, yes, that they're subordinated to the command -- the tactical operative group of Prijedor of the light Brigade of Bosanski Novi, Sanski Most, and Prijedor. I think that this pertains to the 6th Krajina Brigade, but I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you have a look at paragraph 7. It's the first paragraph on page 2 of the Serbo-Croat and in the English version. It states that, "The commands of these brigades have the obligation up until the 1st of July 1992 to establish contact with the commands of the brigades which are subordinated to them"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at page 1 of this document. In the Serbo-Croat version, it is handwritten, and you can see that this document was distributed to the territorial -- to the regional Territorial Defence of Banja Luka, to the 10th Infantry Brigade -- I'm sorry, to the 10th Division of the infantry, to the 343rd Motorised Brigade, and to the 321st Motorised Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this means, why this was added, this handwritten bit. And I don't know what these designations mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you can see that the 6th Brigade isn't mentioned anywhere; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th Brigade is not mentioned, but under number 4 -- I don't know. I said I didn't know, because Sanski Most is mentioned in the context, in parentheses, the light brigade of Bosanski Novi, Sanski Most and Prijedor. And in Sanski Most, there was only one brigade, the 6th Light Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do agree that the Territorial Defence had these units.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was organised -- the Serb Territorial Defence was organised according to local areas. That is to say that it had its command and it operated together with the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that the units of the Territorial Defence -- of the Serbian Territorial Defence were separated from the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to some military type of establishment, yes, possibly. The Territorial Defence -- or rather, the staff of the Territorial Defence had its units, and the 6th Krajina Brigade operated with its own formation. However, when the aggression against Sanski Most took place, there was a joint command according to battalions. That is to say that there were these battalions -- as I said at the outset -- or rather, as I learned, what I could have known, that is, at first there was one particular type of establishment. And when it was over, when the entire territory was taken over, then there was a different type of establishment. At a point there were even 10 or 12 battalions, but all of this was within the 6th Krajina Brigade. I'm not a military expert. I repeat that once again. Perhaps somebody else could speak about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you allow for the possibility that in May 1992 the Territorial Defence was separate from the 6th Brigade? If you don't know, you can simply say that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They operated together; that is to say according to the same plan and in a synchronised manner. The units of the 6th Krajina Brigade were at certain localities, as were the Territorial Defence units. That is to say that in the Territorial Defence there were people who were mobilised, the Serbs of Sanski Most. Every particular settlement belonged to a certain unit, a certain defence unit. So I allow for that possibility. But they carried out their actions together and in a synchronised manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you'd also allow for the possibility that Nedeljko Anicic was a commander of these Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I said that in my statement. He was commander of the Territorial Defence staff. And the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade at that time was Colonel Branko Basara. I think that both of them were later in the Crisis Staff, in the War Staff, as it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 15th of May -- it's page 34 of the LiveNote -- you said that the SOS forces were under the command of the 6th Brigade. How did you know that the SOS forces were under the command of the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, I said where the SOS unit was located. I also said that there was an intervention platoon. I also said that from day one they took part in the attack on Sanski Most in a synchronised manner, together with the 6th Krajina Brigade. On the basis of what I know, if you should put it that way, in Mahala, where my house is, the members of the SOS took part in this and also the members of the army, the members of the 6th Krajina Brigade. That's why I thought that they were a formation which in a way was subordinated to the 6th Krajina Brigade, because in some documents I also saw that Tomo Delic was, according to the establishment pattern, appointed commander of the SOS. And on the other hand, he was in the 4th Battalion of the 6th Krajina Brigade, in that command, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall return to Delic Tomo a little later. Could you now have a look at your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the statement of the 3rd of July, 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 13, the paragraph that precedes the note -- [In English] "14 April 2000." [Interpretation] You earlier stated that: [In English] "I believe that the SOS was the intervention mechanism of the SDS and the Crisis Staff." [Interpretation] Could you say now whether in April and May 1992 the SOS forces were under the command of the SDS or were they under the command of the army?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were under the command of the SDS and the Crisis Staff, that is to say the Crisis Staff and the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you allow for the possibility that it wasn't under the command of the army.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for that period that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few minutes earlier you spoke about Tomo Delic, and you said that he was the commander of the 4th Battalion of the 6th Brigade. Would you agree that he was the commander of the 4th Battalion of a Territorial Defence unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Fauveau. When he mentioned the commander in relation to Tomo Delic, he said that he was appointed commander of the SOS. But with regard to the battalion, he just said that he was in the 4th Battalion of the 6th Krajina Brigade in that command. That's the word he used. He didn't say that he was a commander of the 6th Krajina -- of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he -- I mean, let me put the question to you, Judge. Was he the commander of the 4th Battalion of a Territorial Defence unit? That was the question that Madam Fauveau put to you.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] The commander of the 4th Battalion was Ostoja Cukovic [phoen]; that is to say, a different person.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, Mr. President, you are quite right. What I wanted to know: Would you allow for the possibility that this 4th Battalion in which Tomo Delic participated, was it in fact a Territorial Defence unit, a Serbian Territorial Defence unit?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Battalion was within the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? I didn't hear your question in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that the 4th Battalion in which Tomo Delic was a member was part of the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly where the command was located, or rather, the forward command of that battalion. And I know -- all these people, they are my neighbours from certain neighbourhoods on the other bank of the Sana River, that is to say people who were members of the 4th Battalion. I know that that battalion within the 6th Krajina Brigade went to theatres of war in other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I know -- I have friends until the present day who were members of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that they went to other fronts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that it was after the 1st of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you allow for the possibility that before the 1st of July, 1992 this battalion belonged to the Serbian Territorial Defence of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard for me to answer this question because the military organisation was undergoing changes. I really am not an expert, so I cannot answer all your questions. As for the organisation of the 6th Krajina Brigade and the Territorial Defence -- the Serb Territorial Defence, because there were frequent changes in organisation and in command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I understand your position very well. If you don't know the answer, I'll be quite happy with you saying that you don't know about this. I'll ask you the question once more, and if you don't know the answer, please say so. Would you allow for the possibility that before the 1st of July, 1992 the 4th Battalion belonged to the Serbian Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it belonged to the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think so, but you're not sure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 24th of April -- it's page 4922 -- you mention the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Do you know who the members of the regional Crisis Staff were?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard about some people but not everybody. I know that General Momir Talic was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 did you know that General Talic was a member of the regional Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, did I know? I can't remember. But I assumed so. I know some other members of the Crisis Staff. I knew that the most important people in the region and according to the posts they held were on that staff. I knew Mr. Stojan Zupljanin very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when this Crisis Staff was established?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't know right now. It's hard to remember all of that. I assumed that this was sometime in April. Was it April 1992? But these are just assumptions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say how you knew who the members of the Crisis Staff were?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard, for example, about Kupresanin, about Mr. Brdjanin, General Talic. How I found out, I can't remember now. I probably had information because I did my job until the very end. I didn't want to leave my job, until this Crisis Staff did not, under quotation marks, resolve this -- or rather, until they would dismiss me, because when speaking to Mr Nedeljko Rasula, he mentioned the Crisis Staff from Banja Luka, the Autonomous Region, because I had conversations with Rasula at the critical time in April and May until I was thrown out of the court. As a matter of fact, it is possible that as far back as then I saw some documents, some information about actions taken by certain authorities. Furthermore, there were press releases over TV, that is, because I think that programmes were broadcast only from Banja Luka or Belgrade. There were also some statements that were broadcast over the radio. But indeed, this was ten years ago, and it's hard for me to be very accurate on all of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 24th of April -- it's page 4916 -- you said that two other Muslim judges who worked with you left the town in the month of April 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After they had left, were there any other Muslim judges apart from yourself in the court's building?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the regular court but in the misdemeanours court. That's a different authority altogether. Nedzad Muhic -- Mr. Nedzad Muhic was there and nobody else. I beg your pardon. Azra Alajbegovic was there, but she had also left before. That is to say, she escaped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were forced to leave the court on the 15th of May. And when this took place, was anyone else forced to leave the court at the same time?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said in my statement that I was forced to leave. The president of the misdemeanour's court, Mr. Nedzad Muhic was forced to leave, then the deputy municipal prosecutor, Mr. Enver Ceric; and the registrar of my court, Agan Dzafic, he's a Bosniak too. On the same day at the same meeting that they held -- they held this meeting -- and they communicated this to us, that we were to leave the court premises straight away and that these positions would be taken by ethnic Serbs. Stanic Radovan became president of the municipal court. Andja Vujinic, she became president of the municipal court for misdemeanours. As for Deputy Prosecutor, Rajko Indjic was appointed. And Milenko Delic was appointed prosecutor. That was on the 15th of May, 1992 at 9.00 a.m. until 10.00. The building of the court was sealed off by the army and the police. They were armed. They had automatic rifles. Vladko Vrkes came too. On behalf of the Crisis Staff, he brought in an order, a decision, in writing and he communicated it to us in courtroom number 8, on the ground floor. After that, escorted by the army and the police, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've heard all this before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, you're probably watching me as I am --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's -- Judge, I have to stop you. The question was a very simple one. It said: "You were forced to leave the court on the 15th of May. And when this took place, was anyone else forced to leave the court at the same time?" The answer is yes or no. And if it's yes, you indicate the names of others that were forced. But that's it. I mean, otherwise -- I mean, you are the only witness that I did not address in a very simple way. I have addressed all other witnesses at the beginning by telling them please answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question, because otherwise you will stay here for weeks and weeks and weeks. We don't want the whole story. We just want you to answer the questions that are put to you sometimes by the Prosecution; other times by the Defence. But restrict yourself -- limit yourself to answering those questions, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you have, in fact. Yes. Yes, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said at the hearing of the 24th of April that you had been arrested by a military patrol which was in a yellow Mercedes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a passenger vehicle, a white Golf with another friend, an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at your statement of the 20th of August, 2001. On page 2 of this statement, you said that: [In English] "I was arrested on the 25th May 1992 at my house."

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But not in the house. Near the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You identified the people who had arrested you as members of the military police. If you return to your statement of October 1999 -- I think it's the first statement. On page 11 of this statement -- on page 11 of this statement, you identified the persons --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Oh. This statement -- now I really don't know. Could you please repeat this to me. Which statement is this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement of the 29th and the 30th of October, 1999. And it's on page 11. You spoke about your arrest.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not the document. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the statement of the 29th and 30th of October with translation number 00873132, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unfortunately I did not bother to bring the Serbo-Croat versions with me today, so I can't help the witness much.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 11 of this statement, you spoke about your arrest and you identified the persons who had arrested you. You said they were Danilusko Kajtez, Bato Vukic, Vlasto Vidovic, and Milorad Krunic. Do you stand by your statement?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that Milorad Krunic was a member of the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Krunic was retired. He was a retired policeman. At that time he was appointed warden of the prison. I don't know which prison though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in any case, he was not a member of the military police. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Possibly he was not a member. But he knew me very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 25th of April -- it's page 4972 -- you said that you had been searched after you arrived at the police station in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to give the policeman the objects in your possession?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was frisked by a policeman. I gave him -- I think I gave him all my things, my documents. I had my ID there. I had my driver's licence. Also the licence of my vehicle. And I had my bank card and my cheque-book. I gave him all of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to keep some of the items that you had on you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only kept the key to my house. I kept it in my pocket. I had some money too, a little bit of money, and I kept that, very little money. I had very little money on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the policeman know that you had this money?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible he did know. Possibly he saw it. When I took everything out, he saw it possibly, because he searched all my pockets. But the money was taken away from me at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you detained all the time from the time when you were arrested up until the time when you departed for Manjaca? Were you detained this entire time in the police station?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 24th of April -- it's page 4979 -- you said that during your detention in Sanski Most, you went to get some water. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
